analytic.title: Hard Real-Time Scheduling on a Multicore Platform

div.p: MuIticore microcontrollers are rapidly penetrating the real-time systems market with a promise of increased pro cessing throughput and lower energy consumption compared to traditional single-core processors. Consequently, it sparked a wave of research in Soft Real-Time (SRT) scheduling algorithms for muIticore processors producing many different scheduling algorithms that are good at harnessing the added power of the multicore processors but lack the required determinism to be used in Hard Real-Time (HRT) systems. We present the MuIticore Priority Ceiling Protocol scheduling algorithm for HRT systems along with its schedulability test for HRT systems running on a single instance of a modified RTOS. We also developed a tool that uses our schedulability test to solve the task partitioning problem using a Particle Swarm Optimization.
' A scheduling algorithm is said to be optimal if it always produces feasible schedules when feasible schedules exist.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the world of software, one can categorize a system as either being real-time or non real-time. A system is said to be real-time if the output of a calculation is as important as the time at which the output is delivered by the system [ 1]. Common desktop software is not considered real-time as it is expected to behave according to the minimum response time and the proportionality of service principle. In other words, on a desktop system, there is usually no specified timing constraints for specific output and a user will expect longer delays depending on the task being performed and system load. Most embedded systems, on the other hand, are considered to be real-time as they often interact with the physical world and must therefore respect different timing constraints to work properly.
In [1], Liu defines a model to reason about real-time systems where a system is divided into tasks that have certain properties. A real-time task has the following properties:
• p: A period (this is the specified amount of time between the release of each job of a task)
• e: A worst case execution time (The longest amount of time a job may need the processor to complete)

• d: A deadline (the time at which a job must be finished to be considered valid; if no deadline is specified, the period of the task is used as the deadline meaning that the job must be completed before the next job is released) According to Liu, this model is practical for the analysis of most real-time systems. By analysis, we mean the mathemati cal verification that every task in the system will always meet all its deadlines under any circumstance. Such validation is called a schedulability analysis and it is a very important step of any serious HRT system design.

The mathematics to formally analyse the schedulability on single core processor real-time systems have been available in the literature for over thirty years and, more recently, have been adapted to mUltiprocessor systems. However, this transition to multiprocessors was not trivial and is still the subject of significant research to try and reach an optimal ' scheduling algorithm. Some algorithms show good theoretical promise but actually perform very poorly on today's hardware [2] , [3]. In the meantime, the industry is in need of a proven, deterministic algorithm that can harness the promises of multicores while offering the formal verification of the schedulability of a system.

Our contributions to the field are a new scheduling algo rithm for Multicore Hard Real-Time Systems (MHRTS) as well as the schedulability test necessary to perform the schedula bility analysis. We also compare our algorithm to its more complicated predecessor algorithm derived by Rajkumar and published in 1990 [4] . Although this may seem like an outdated paper, Rajkumar's model and theory are still very relevant in terms of shared memory multiprocessor HRT systems. How ever, in 1990, shared memory multiprocessor systems were not as closely coupled as the ubiquitous multicore processors which led us to believe that Rajkumar's algorithm could further be optimized for tightly coupled multicore architectures. This paper is divided into three parts first covering the background and motivations behind our work in sec tions II and III followed by a complete description of the scheduling algorithm we are introducing in this paper along with its associated schedulability testing section IV. We con clude the paper with a comparison between our algorithm with the current solutions in section VI.

div.head: II. PREDICTABILITY AND DETERMINISM
div.p: When dealing with real-time systems, one has to identify the level of criticality with which each task has to meet its deadlines. If one or more tasks in the system would lead to catastrophic consequences if it missed its deadline, the real time system is called an HRT system [1] . In general, this type of system sacrifices scheduling power for determinism. This means that the system will ultimately be able to run less tasks than an SRT system and will be less flexible but will be analyzable in terms of timings. Examples of HRT systems are aircrafts, nuclear reactors, most weapon systems, some automobile systems and more. Examples of SRT systems are mobile phones, electronic thermostats and most electronic consumer products. When building a HRT system, a designer will need to use a RTOS system that is deterministic. HRT operating systems usually achieve this by not allowing tasks to migrate from one core to the other also referred to as partitioned as well as using fixed priorities for all tasks along with a proper priority assignment algorithm off-line. SRT systems tend to focus more on flexibility and scheduling power and usually achieve it by allowing tasks to migrate from one core to the other also referred to as global and by using dynamic priority schemes. Fig. 1 shows the distribution of the algorithms along those two axis.

div.head: III. CURRENT SOLUTIONS
div.p: As of today, multiprocessor HRT systems are still designed using the end-to-end task model for distributed systems where tasks are subdivided into subtasks that are distributed onto the different processors as described in [5] . In this model, resources such as sensors or other specific hardware are physically bound to a specific processor in the system and when a task requires a specific resource it must run its critical section on the associated processor. The system being distributed, an RTOS must run on every processor in the system and communication is done via messages. The system then runs as a carefully choreographed set of tasks of multiple processors exchanging messages at run-time in order to meet all its end-to end deadlines. This approach is analyzable and proven and is therefore currently preferred by the HRT system architects. The trend is to emulate a distributed system on multicore platforms in order use the end-to-end approach. Obviously this technique is offers a reassuring continuity but it is not taking advantage of the closely coupled processors on a multicore hardware architecture where a level of cache is shared for inter processor communication.

If dealing with a shared memory multiprocessor system, an HRT system designer could also have used the task syn chonization protocol for multiprocessor systems developed by Rajkumar in 1990. However, this option never really material ized because shared memory multiprocessor systems in the 90s were mainly designed for high performance computing such as the Cray and SGI machines and never really got into the HRT domain. Today, with multicore processors being shared cache multiprocessor systems, such a solution would be a real option. Our research aims at offering this new option specifically for the multicore platform.

div.head: IV. DE FINITION OF THE MULTICORE PRIORITY CEILING
PROTOCOL
div.p: In this section, we introduce the Multicore Priority Ceiling Protocol (MCPCP) as a solution for developing HRT systems on multicore platforms. The algorithm was tailored to meet the main objectives listed bellow. We also derived a sufficient schedulability test that allows the system engineers to verify that their systems will always meet their deadlines.

div.head: A. Objectives
div.p: We defined our objectives for the scheduling algorithm based on several discussions with Micrium Inc making sure we were in touch with the current HRT industry requirements. Those objectives are behind all the decisions that were made when defining the rules of our algorithm found in Section IV-B.
The scheduling algorithm shall be deterministic 2 .

The scheduling algorithm shall support a simple tran sition of previous single core systems to multicore by not requiring system designers to perform extra tasks such as subdividing the tasks into subtasks based on resource usage.
The scheduling algorithm shall support easy modifi cations and additions to the system.

div.head: B. Scheduling algorithm rules
div.p: A realistic multicore scheduling algorithm has to precisely define the rules that will determine when a task is allowed to run and when it is preempted to let another task run. It also defines how resources are managed and shared from task to task. Bellow is the list of rules we developed that define the MCPCP scheduling algorithm:

The algorithm divides tasks into partitions that are bound to a specific processor. This task assignment is done off-line and may not change at runtime. This type of scheduling algorithm is cOlmnonly referred to as a partitioned system in the literature and although normally less powerful than their counterpart global algorithm [6], they benefit in determinism by avoiding the cold cache problem [3].

The algorithm is priority driven in that the highest priority task of each partition that is ready is always executing (Greedy scheduler). For the purpose of this paper, lower numerical values (including negative values) indicate higher priorities.

All tasks have a priority assigned using the Dead line Monotonic Priority Ordering (DMPO) algorithm. The DMPO priority assignment has been shown to be optimal for the single processor static priority scheduling algorithm [7]. Although it has been shown not to be the case for multiprocessor systems [6], our partitioned approach is enssentially a collection of single processor systems sharing resources through shared memory.

All critical sections are of higher priority than the highest task's priority in the system. In a system with n tasks, the critical section's priority of task Ti where 1 :s; i :s; n, 'ITi,CS is equal to the priority of Ti minus the value of the lowest priority in the system hence elevating its priority higher than the highest priority while keeping the same relative priority between critical sections. A task executing a critical section can preempt an other task executing a different critical section if its priority is higher.
All resources Rk have a request queue (Qk) that is ordered by each task's critical section priorities ('IT = 'ITi -'ITlowest ). The highest priority task in Q k gets the resource when it is freed.
Critical section nesting is not permitted and only one resource per critical section is allowed.

All critical sections are global critical sections mean ing that no difference is made between a resource being used by tasks that all co-reside on the same partition or not 3 . This rule contrasts with Rajkumar's scheduling algorithm [4] where resources had to be bound to a processor due to the loose nature of shared memory systems of the early 1990's era and where the I/O was not necessarily memory mapped. This rule is therefore a relaxation allowed by the close proximity of the processors on a multicore system where all cores have equal access to all resources of the system with uniform latency.

div.head: C. Assumptions and notation
div.p: Our algorithm is specifically designed for multicore pro cessors thus allowing us to make the following assumptions:
• The architecture of the system ensures cache coher ence through the use of a snooping protocol or other appropriate techniques [8] .
3 From this point in the paper, we will refer to global critical sections as critical sections since we do not have the concept of local critical sections in our algorithm.
The latency for synchronization activities is negligible [ 1] .
The RTOS executes on one of the cores and either requires a negligible amount of processor time to execute or its processor utilization is factored in the tasks executing on the same processor.

div.head: D. Schedulability test
div.p: A schedulability test may be used at run-time or pre-run time depending on the nature of the real-time system being designed. If the system must admit new real-time tasks at runtime, it must first test if this new task may jeopardize the schedulability of the system at which point it may decide to accept or refuse to admit the new task. However, simply exe cuting the test requires precious time itself generally justifying the use of a pessimistic heuristic bound calculation. Since run time addition of tasks is, by definition, non-deterministic, it is unsuitable for Hard Real-Time Systems (HRTS). Our research being focused on HRTS, we do not allow modifications of the taskset at runtime. This restriction allowed us to develop a much less pessimistic but more computationally intensive schedulability test that we run off-line. Furthermore, our system being partitioned, we actually use our schedulability test in the fitness function of our search algorithm to find a solution to the task partitioning problem.
The remainder of this section describes the schedulability test for our new scheduling algorithm. The notation used follows that of Liu [1] and is explained when new symbols are introduced.

div.head: E. Blocking Scenarios
div.p: The identification of the blocking scenarios that may occur when an HRTS is executing using the MCPCP scheduling algorithm was one of the main tasks of this research. Another was to properly represent each blocking scenario mathemat ically to be able to incorporate them in the schedulability test. It is important to note that we cannot prove that all possible blocking scenarios have been identified and thus there could be some extra obscure blocking scenario(s) that may still remain to be discovered. It will become apparent through the remainder of this section that the mathematical representations of the blocking scenarios are pessimistic as they must represent the worst case even if this worst case may probably never happen. We provide simple, explicit examples of worst case scenarios that may occur in a system executing using the MCPCP sheduling algorithm to help the reader understand the model. In some cases, a simpler example is also given to show the essence of the blocking scenario being discussed.

div.head: 1) Local Blocking Time (LBT):
div.p: LBT captures all the time a task may be blocked by other local tasks. Since any local higher priority tasks are considered interference and taken into account by equation ( 4), only the critical sections of local lower priority tasks are to be considered. The worst case of this blocking scenario is captured based on the logic used by Rajkumar for his scheduling algorithm [4] which also exhibited local blocking. The worst case is as follow: after each job of Ti is released, it may be blocked once by each lower priority local task that has a critical section. Moreover, each time it uses a resource, Ti potentially gives up the processor due to the resource being locked by a remote task (although this is another blocking scenario called remote blocking, it influences the worst case for LBT by potentially allowing a local lower priority task to execute and lock a resource before Ti is remotely unblocked). Each time Ti is blocked, it may be blocked by the longest critical section of each of the lower priority tasks. Our algorithm is partitioned meaning that it requires every task to be assigned to a processor and that no migration is allowed at run-time. Assigning the task optimally in order to minimize the number of cores required for the system to be schedulable has been shown to be NP-Hard from a reduction of the bin packing problem [9] . We therefore reconunend solving for a solution using a heuristic algorithm such as a Genetic Algorithm or the Particle Swarm Optimization[1O] .

We developed such a tool using the particle swarm opti mization algorithm to find a solution to the task partitioning problem based on the schedulability test seen in the previous section. We evaluate the fitness of a partitioning solution by sUlmning the amount of tasks that could meet their deadline weighted for their priority. This ensures that a solution suc cessfully scheduling higher priority tasks will be considered better than a solution scheduling the same amount of lower priority tasks.
We then used this tool to compare our algorithm with its predecessor Task Synchronization protocol from Rajkumar [ 4] .

div.head: VI. COMPARING MCPCP WITH THE RE AL-TIME TASK SYNCHRONIZATION PROTOCOL FROM RAJKUMAR
div.p: Our thesis for this research was that we could simplify Rajkumars Task Synchronization Protocol [4] by removing the concept of local and global resources along with all its associ ated rules and by making all resources global. This makes the MCPCP scheduling algorithm much simpler to implement in an RTOS as well as having a lower run-time overhead. This modification also simplifies the schedulability test and reduces the overlap between the blocking scenarios.

We compared the scheduling power of the MCPCP scheduling algorithm with the more complex task synchro nization protocol from Rajkumar to verify our thesis. The comparison was done by randomly generating more than eleven thousand different task sets using the Java Emitter Template (JET) and then finding the lowest number of cores required to schedule the task set using both algorithms.

A more powerful algorithm would require less cores to schedule a given task set than a less powerful scheduling algorithm. We randomly generated 11707 different task sets with varying properties in terms of number of tasks, number of shared resources, number of critical sections, total task utilization and total critical section utilization. Of those 11707 total task utilisation bins Fig. 8. Distribution of the total task utilization for the sample taskset containing 28 tasks randomly generated task sets, 7576 were schedulable by at least one of the two algorithms. As an example of the range of values used in our random taskset generator, we plotted the distribution of the tasksets in terms of their total task utilization (Figure 8) as well as for the number of critical sections (Figure 9). The X axis in Figure 8 represents different classification bins for all the generated tasksets that had 28 tasks based on the total task utilization. The height of the bins indicate how many tasksets got classified in that bin. It essentially shows that we varied task utilization enough to obtain tasksets that represented many very small tasks as well as many very large tasks. Note that the histogram only contain the taskset that were actually schedulable on at least on algorithm explaining why the bins get smaller the higher the utilization. Figure 9 serves a similar purpose but with the total number of critical sections instead of total task utilization. The number of critical section is an important factor in terms of a real-time system task set complexity and increases the difficulty to successfully schedule the system. Again, we see that the higher the number of critical sections, the lower the bins meaning that the tasksets with lots of critical sections were more difficult to schedule using either scheduling algorithm. Figure 10 gives the results of our analysis where the x axis represents the size of the task sets in number of tasks and the bars are the median values of the number of cores required to successfully schedule the system by each algorithm.

We can see that the Rajkumar's algorithm has almost identical performance when compared to the MCPCP. In order to confirm this, we performed a statistical test. Since the distributions were not normal, we could not apply one of the standard tests such as the T-test. Therefore, we applied a non-parametric test to assess the equality of the distributions, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Our test was performed with a significance level of 1 %(a = 0.01). For all the generated sizes of the tasksets (4 to 48), the null hypothesis (that the distributions for Rajkumar's algorithm and the MCPCP are the same) failed to be rejected. Therefore we may conclude that both algorithms have a statistically identical performance.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: This research aimed at providing a simpler scheduling algorithm for HRT systems running on multi-core platforms. We defined this algorithm with simplicity and the advantages of multi-core processors in mind and then proceeded to model the different blocking scenarios that could arise. The blocking scenarios represent the bulk of this research as it is at the heart of our schedulability analysis formula. A tool solving the task partitioning problem was also developed based on our schedulability test and was used to compare our solution with its predecessor scheduling algorithm called the shared memory task synchronization protocol developed by Rajkumar et al. This partitioning tool will be presented in a future paper. Our tests have shown that our algorithm achieves compara ble scheduling power while being simpler to implement in an RTOS. We can therefore say that this research provides an interesting option to HRT system design that requires a predictable and analyzable system.
